pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps reply lines at 16 characters. As a result, most success paths can't be reached, and the code that parses the control port (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) never runs.

This rewrites the target around a fake Tor on the other end of a real `TorControlConnection`, connected through `DynSock`. Replies go over the wire. The fake Tor answers each command the controller sends with a reply of the matching shape, so inputs can complete the whole handshake: PROTOCOLINFO, authentication (including SAFECOOKIE), GETINFO and ADD_ONION. The harness also checks that reply data never splits a command or injects a new one.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`, which deleted its own socket. The bug has been there since #30205; this target is the first caller.

### Testing

Line coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp` goes from 52% on master to 81% after a 10-minute local run. The master number is from the qa-assets corpus. Most of what remains is the controller thread itself, which the harness replaces, and socket errors that `DynSock` can't produce.

The input format changes, so the corpus in qa-assets needs a refresh.

pulls.title: wallet, bdbro: Reject overflow pages without data
pulls.body:
`BerkeleyRODatabase::Open` reads an overflow record by following `next_page` until it is 0. #34959 added a check that stops once more data than `item_len` was read, which needs every page to add data. An overflow page with `hf_offset` 0 adds none. If such a page names itself as `next_page`, the loop reads it again and again and never ends.

This PR treats an overflow page without data as corruption.

**Behavior change:** a file with an empty overflow page no longer opens and fails with `Overflow page has no data`. Before, an empty page with `next_page` 0 was accepted and the record came out shorter than `item_len`.

**Measurement:** regtest, RelWithDebInfo, base a527a0077a. The file has 5 pages of 4096 bytes: one key whose value is an overflow record with `item_len` 100, and one overflow page.

| overflow page | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hf_offset` 0, `next_page` itself | `bitcoin-wallet dump` at 100 % of one core, killed after 60 s | fails at once, exit 1 |
| `hf_offset` 100, `next_page` 0 | dumped in 0.11 s | dumped as before |

With `migratewallet` on master the RPC does not return and one HTTP worker stays at 100 % CPU. Other RPCs still answer, but `stop` had not finished after 30 s.

**Tests:** new case in `tool_wallet.py` that writes both files by hand. On master it hangs (killed after 90 s). Passing locally: `test_bitcoin` and `test_runner.py` with the default list. Not run: fuzz targets, lint.

Contributed by [turingpoint](https://www.turingpoint.de).

qt: don't abort or drop settings when dynamic settings are disabled
pulls.body:
`ArgsManager::WriteSettingsFile` throws when dynamic settings are disabled, and three call sites in `NodeImpl` call it without checking first. So `bitcoin-qt -nosettings` aborts on `-resetguisettings`, and on the legacy GUI settings migration when an old Qt setting is still present, which comes back on every start because the abort happens before the key is removed.

The fourth call site in that file is the wallet path in `ChainImpl`, and #36176 guards it. These three are the options dialog, and I ran into them while testing that PR.

The flag is easier to reach than it looks, since the fatal error box suggests `-nosettings` when the settings file cannot be written.

Guarding the writes on its own is not enough, because three things then happen silently instead of aborting. The migration drops the legacy keys, since it removes them whether or not the write landed. The dialog closes reporting success, since `setOption` only reported parse errors and `QDataWidgetMapper::submit()` does not propagate what `setData` returns. And it asks for a restart that would discard the change rather than apply it, which is reachable today without the flag.

`bitcoin-qt -regtest -nosettings -resetguisettings` aborts on master and starts here. The Qt tests cover the guards and each of those, with settings disabled and with a write that fails, and each one fails without its change.

The second commit reports rather than fixes the abort, so it can be dropped if reviewers would rather keep this to the crash.

are also tracked in mapBlocksInFlight. The condition that decides
whether a new block is requested as a compact block counted those

kernel: Use typed errors for fatal and flush error notifications
pulls.body:
Part of the libbitcoinkernel project (tracking issue #27587 ), specifically the "Remove translation.h usage from the kernel" item. `kernel::Notifications::fatalError()` and `flushError()` take a `bilingual_str`, which pulls `util/translation.h` and the application-level `G_TRANSLATION_FUN` into the kernel library, and translation is an application concern rather than a consensus one. The same interface already shows the way out: `warningSet()` takes a `kernel::Warning` enum, and the node turns it into a translated string in `node/kernel_notifications.cpp`.

Along with removing the dependency, another goal here is separating responsibilities, because the goals of error handling and error reporting are different: presenting an error to a user is an application concern, not something `libbitcoinkernel` itself should own. The error is structured on both sides: in C++ as the full `kernel::FatalError` variant, and in the C API as its numeric value. With the current changes the C side only carries half of that structure today though, the dynamic fields (a block hash, a path, an exception's `what()`) do not cross the C API yet, even though ideally they should.

This PR does the same for the two error notifications. A new `src/kernel/error.h` defines `kernel::FlushError` as a plain enum and `kernel::FatalError` as a `std::variant` with one struct per error, whose fields carry the context the message needs: a block hash, a path, the `what()` of a caught exception, block heights. It holds types and nothing else, so every message is now built on the node side. The exception is `FatalErrorString()` in `validation.cpp`, because a fatal error raised during validation also fails the block through `BlockValidationState::Error()`, which takes the reason as a plain string right there, and `fatalError()` returns void, so the node has no way to put its message into that state. A follow-up could store the typed error in the state instead and let the node create the string message.

This does not remove the kernel's dependency on `util/translation.h`, it is just a step. The other two notifications, `progress()` and `warningSet()`, still take a `bilingual_str`, and `bitcoinkernel.cpp`, `checks.cpp`, `node/chainstate.cpp`, `txmempool.cpp` and `validation.cpp` still include the header.

There is one behavior change to mention here. The two C API callbacks lose their `message` parameter, so they now carry only the error code, the same pattern that `btck_BlockValidationResult` already uses.

pulls.title: wallet: start descriptor top up at range_start instead of index 0
pulls.body:
DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::TopUpWithDB() expands the descriptor from m_max_cached_index + 1, which is 0 for a freshly imported descriptor regardless of its range_start. Importing a descriptor with "range": [N, M] therefore derives and watches every index in [0, M), so the cost of an import is O(M) rather than O(M - N) and the wallet treats scriptPubKeys below N as its own. Load() only expands [range_start, range_end), so those scriptPubKeys stop being IsMine the next time the wallet is opened, and a transaction picked up for one of them during the import rescan is no longer credited to the wallet.

Since ParseDescriptorRange() only bounds the size of the range and not its start, "range": [2146483648, 2147483647] is accepted and expands 2^31 indexes into m_map_script_pub_keys before the RPC returns.

Start the top up loop at range_start and record the index that was actually cached instead of counting from -1, so that Load() and TopUpWithDB() agree on m_max_cached_index for descriptors with a non-zero range_start. Before this change Load() left m_max_cached_index at range_end - range_start - 1 for such descriptors, which made the first top up after opening the wallet re-expand the stored range.

Importing wpkh(xpub/0/*) with "range": [600000, 600009] into a blank watch-only wallet goes from 19.5s to 0.09s on this machine.

pulls.title: p2p: serve and fetch stale-branch blocks (BIP 332)(Stale Tip Relay)
pulls.body:
Part of #36833. 
Based on #36920; review from `refactor: extract block serving limit checks`.

This PR lets peers fetch the blocks behind the stale tips announced in #36920. We now serve blocks on the stale branches we track, and the new -staletips=blocks mode downloads the branches peers offer.

### Key changes

* `-staletips=blocks` advertises `prefers_blocks=true` and fetches offered branches. For peers that prefer blocks, we wait to announce a tip until we've fetched it, unless the fetch stalls.
* Fetches are best-effort and separate from normal block download:
  * They start at the tip, since that's all `have_block` promises.
  * Each block is requested from one peer at a time, and only while that peer has fewer than 8 blocks in flight.
* This also fixes how #36920 handles a higher-work `staletip`. It used to go through normal block download, which expected every ancestor from that peer and could disconnect it. Now it's fetched best-effort, in both modes.

pulls.title: p2p: Relay stale tip announcements (BIP 332)(Stale Tip Relay)
pulls.body:
Part of #36833.
Based on #36919; review from `p2p: add staletip message type and payload`.

This adds the [BIP 332](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0332.md) `staletip` message, negotiated through the BIP 434 `BIP332` feature. With `-staletips=headers`, the node announces the stale tips it tracks and tracks the ones its peers announce. Only headers are relayed.

### Key changes

* New `staletip` message type and payload.
* Add a `StaleTipRelayManager`, which holds the relay policy.
* With `-staletips=headers`, the node advertises `BIP332` (with `prefers_blocks=false`) and relays only with peers that advertise it too.
* Stale tips learned from peers are tracked, and listed by `getchaintips` with `staletips_only`:

  <details>
  <summary>Sample output</summary>

  A node that learned of a stale tip only from a peer's `staletip` message:

  ```
  $ bitcoin-cli -named getchaintips staletips_only=true

      "status": "headers-only"
    }
  ]
  ```

  </details>

* `getnetworkinfo` gets a `localfeatures` field, listing the BIP 434 features the node advertises.

  <details>

  ```
  $ bitcoin-cli getnetworkinfo
  {
    ...
    "localfeatures": {
      "BIP332": {
        "prefers_blocks": false
      }
    },
    ...
  }
  ```

  </details>

* `getpeerinfo` gets a `features` field, listing the BIP 434 features each peer advertises.

pulls.title: addrman: don't stall feelers when a tried collision is unreachable
pulls.body:
When the old entry in a collision is unreachable and hasn't connected successfully in the last 4 hours, it can only leave the collision set through the 40-minute `ADDRMAN_TEST_WINDOW` branch. Until then, if it's the only pending collision, no feeler connections are made at all.
This is a rare occurrence I ran into when I switched from dual-homed (IPv4 + Tor) to `-onlynet=ipv4`.

`ThreadOpenConnections()` repeatedly calls `SelectTriedCollision()`, which keeps returning the unreachable entry. Since its network is unreachable, the entry is skipped without making a connection. `nTries` eventually runs out without any feeler connections being made.
The same process repeats on subsequent feeler turns until `ResolveCollisions()` resolves the collision after `ADDRMAN_TEST_WINDOW` (40 minutes).

This PR passes the reachable networks to `SelectTriedCollision()`, so it only returns collisions whose to-be-evicted entry belongs to a reachable network.
If none of the pending collisions qualify, nothing is returned, and a regular feeler connection is made instead.

Another approach I considered [2](https://github.com/naiyoma/bitcoin/pull/25) is to overwrite unreachable tried entries involved in a collision directly in `ResolveCollisions()`.

pulls.title: p2p: Track recent stale tips (BIP 332)(Stale Tip Relay)
pulls.body:
Part of #36833

This PR adds local tracking of recent stale tips for [BIP 332](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0332.md).
The feature is behind a new `-staletips=<mode>` option (default `none`). There is no P2P change yet: with `-staletips=headers` the node only tracks tips.

### Key changes

* A new `AcceptedStaleTip` validation notification feeds the staletips tracker.
* The tracker is built from the block index at startup, keeping the tips with the most work.
  *  At most 10 tips are tracked. When the tracker is full, a new tip evicts the one with the least work, but only if the new tip has more work.
* `getchaintips` RPC updates
  * Add new options `max_depth` and `staletips_only`
  * Report `fork_point` for each non-active tip.

Test networks get the stricter policies the BIP recommends:
* **signet:** only tips whose block has been validated, and one header variant per block. 
* **testnet3/4:** only tips with a difficulty of at least about 1,000,000.

pulls.title: test: Add debug output to common tested types
pulls.body:
If the `<<` operator exists, boost can use this as a debug output when a check fails (besides `BOOST_CHECK`). This adds `<<` for types commonly used across the unit tests that do not yet have a display output. Each callsite that uses these types are then updated to use macros that will print the debug output on failure. All of these display strings would be used as part of #35713, but we can also use them with boost today.

What this PR does:
- Adds debug output for types used across multiple files, or types that have a clear debug string, and migrates the `BOOST_CHECK` calls. This covers the majority of custom types that did not yet have a debug string.

What this PR does _not_ do:
- Migrate `BOOST_CHECK` callsites for types that already _do_ have a debug output (all primitive type comparisons, `CFeeRate`, etc). This would be a much larger refactor and could perhaps be done after.
- Add debug output for `std::vector<T>` where `T` is streamable. These can be migrated to `BOOST_CHECK_EQUAL_COLLECTIONS`, but is a similar refactor to the one above.
- Add debug output for `std::vector<unsigned char>` and related. Also a large refactor, and could use discussion.
- Add debug output for types that would require a `friend` method in the source code (`ByRatio`)

pulls.title: fuzz: improve ipc fuzz coverage
pulls.body:
This PR follows up on #35118 and continues the IPC fuzzing work proposed in #23015.

The initial ipc fuzz target exercised normal calls through a libmultiprocess client and server. This PR extends the target with

 - Server side assertions that verify arguments arrive unchanged (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#issuecomment-4452992198 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#pullrequestreview-4539477599)
 - A callback call that exercises ipc communication in both directions.
 - Raw capnp requests containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess server.
  - Raw capnp responses containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess client.

The raw request and response cases allow the fuzz target to exercise deserialization with data that was not first produced by libmultiprocess serialization.

The ipc setup and callback handling closely follow the existing [`libmultiprocess` tests](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/libmultiprocess/test/mp/test/test.cpp), particularly their use of `EventLoop`, `ProxyClient`, `ProxyServer`, two-way pipes, and `initThreadMap`. 

The transaction and UniValue payload cases exercise the serialization hooks defined in [`common-types.h`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/capnp/common-types.h). 

These files may provide useful background when reviewing the changes.

Generated [coverage report](https://enirox001.github.io/coverage/ipc/) after fuzzing the IPC target for a while using the qa-assets corpus.

pulls.title: btcsignals: destroy callbacks on disconnect
pulls.body:
Currently callback functions connected to signals do not get freed when their `connection::disconnect` method is called or when their associated `scoped_connection` is destroyed. They live as long as the signal does, even if they will never be called, and can only get [garbage collected](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/0fd515bbb7070a502dd2fe6d16f5f3cbac591283/src/util/btcsignals.h#L240-L241) if new connections are added.

This behavior is different that previous boost signals behavior and causes a [deadlock](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/31848571315/job/94919834743) on GUI shutdown in #10102 because when the node registers signal callbacks (`handleInitMessage`, etc) that get forwarded to the GUI, the callbacks own `mp::EventLoopRef` references, and if the callbacks aren't freed, the node process can't shut down.

This change restores boost signals behavior freeing callbacks when they are disconnected or when `scoped_connection` objects are destroyed to avoid this problem and make callback lifetimes more predictable.

pulls.title: mining: add getMemoryLoad() and track template non-mempool memory footprint
pulls.body:
IPC clients can hold block templates indefinitely, keeping transactions alive after they leave the mempool. This adds `getMemoryLoad()` to estimate the memory held on behalf of all mining clients, as discussed in bitcoin/bitcoin#33899. It does not impose a limit.

The estimate includes each tracked template's vectors and the transactions it references that are no longer in the mempool. Transaction objects shared by multiple templates are counted once. Dummy coinbase transactions and the template cached by the `getblocktemplate` RPC are excluded.

`BlockTemplateManager` tracks templates through weak references, so the registry does not prolong their lifetime. Templates unregister when destroyed, including when IPC cleanup happens after shutdown has reset the manager. Clients can reduce the reported memory load by releasing stale templates or explicitly calling `destroy()`.

The result is an estimate: the mempool can change during calculation, and eviction followed by re-entry as a different transaction object can cause undercounting.

Example client usage: [stratum-mining/sv2-tp#63](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp/pull/63).

Commits:

- `refactor: share ownership of BlockTemplateManager`
- `mining: track block templates held by IPC clients`
- `mining: add GetTemplateMemoryUsage()`
- `ipc: add getMemoryLoad()`
- `test: check template memory accounting invariants`

pulls.title: btcsignals: disconnect callbacks when destroying signal
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #36011

When a connection handle outlives its signal, a callback that was still connected at signal destruction stays alive, and the handle continues to report `connected() == true`. The referenced PR fix made an explicit `disconnect()` call release the callback. However, destroying the signal still did not disconnect its callbacks automatically, as pointed out by the author in this [#36011 comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36011#discussion_r4459623066).

This PR's commit disconnects each callback when its signal is destroyed. It extends the `callback_destruction` test to verify that destroying the signal also releases an idle callback’s captured state and the surviving handle gets disconnected, as suggested in this [#36011 comment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36011#discussion_r4459623272).

pulls.body:
## Generatetomany

First approach was to create a `generatetomany` rpc call. That approach can be seen here https://github.com/polespinasa/bitcoin/pull/3

## Generateblock
Modifies `generateblock` to allow a user to set multiple outputs in the coinbase transaction. If an empty set is provided, the block will be empty. If no set of transactions is provided, the block will mine the mempool. If a set of transactions is provided only that set of txs will be mined.

```
$./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock bcrt1qw6qkj8wtw5hraxwxjp08m4aymkntms3yhqyacj

  "hash": "7359a3ed7af0f18f4016e6cb29193bd787a2452c584781135c585d5204b9ec5b"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]'
{
  "hash": "6db028454b26d6667dd6df45be2772844121fb44f86433f6bbfbafa429974684"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]' []

{
  "hash": "33e2ddc52546ddb0edf28bef5b295ee8fbd487b8aca19c97018467e2477877df"
}

```

### Motivation
https://x.com/SuperTestnet/status/1921220086645342550

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author changes from `bad_function_call` to `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration to fail.

The second commit moves the check for an empty `mapWallet` to after `RunWithinTxn()` commits the database transaction and runs the commit callback, when transactions marked for removal have been deleted.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~54 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: mining: move getblocktemplate cache into BlockTemplateManager
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #35675. This addresses the `getblocktemplate` part of the "Remove remaining global states" TODO in #33758, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35675#pullrequestreview-5299625960.

`getblocktemplate` reuses its last template until the tip changes, or until the mempool changes and the template is more than 5 seconds old. That cache currently lives in four function-local statics, which:

- live as long as the process, so the cached `CBlockIndex*` can outlive its `ChainstateManager` (as in unit tests);
- rely on `cs_main` being held, which nothing checks;
- can't be unit tested.

This PR moves the cache into `BlockTemplateManager`, in three commits:

1. **rpc:** refactors the statics in place into a `CachedBlockTemplate` struct and a `GetNewOrCachedBlockTemplate()` helper, `GUARDED_BY(::cs_main)`. The template's `hashPrevBlock` replaces the cached `CBlockIndex*`, and the 5 seconds becomes `GBT_TEMPLATE_REBUILD_INTERVAL`.
2. **refactor:** moves them into `BlockTemplateManager`. It's easiest to review with `git show --color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=allow-indentation-change`.
3. **test:** adds a unit test for each rebuild rule and for the retry after a failed build.

No behavior change is intended, and only `getblocktemplate` uses the cache. It uses `cs_main` rather than its own mutex, since the RPC already holds it and building a template takes it anyway.

pulls.title: validation: prefetch blocks while connecting
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Connecting a block already on disk requires reading and deserializing it.
Doing this on the validation thread stalls validation and slows reindexing and initial block download.

This is a follow-up to [#35295](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35295), which parallelized input prevout fetching during block connection.

**Fix:** Add a `Chainstate`-owned block fetcher that reads later blocks from disk while the current block is connected.
Start with synchronous 1-block read-ahead, then move reads to an eagerly started worker pool that persists across activations.
Keep caller-provided blocks on the direct path and refill a sliding read-ahead window.
During reorgs, start reading the first sibling while disconnecting the old tip.
Retry speculative failures synchronously when the block is needed.

`-blockfetchthreads=<n>` selects readers per chainstate, with a default of 2 and a cap of 16.
Setting it to 0 disables read-ahead. The window retains up to two blocks per reader, giving 4 by default.
Measurements favor 2 readers with a window of 4 or 8 blocks, so the default uses the smaller window.

**Credit:** The idea comes from [bitcoindev1337](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-08-11#1245429), who had already implemented a similar design and reported comparable results.

For more context, see: #36027

Encrypting existing wallets that are unencrypted is fraught with footguns and complexity both for users and for developers.

For example:

- Encrypting a wallet that has manually imported descriptors will cause the wallet to change the spending conditions out from under the user. (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/26607)

- Because new keys are made after encryption, restoring from a backup made before encryption may result in loss of funds.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

`CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. A follow-up #36918 with optimizations improves the worst case deserialization time significantly instead. Other minor degradations:
* libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
* `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: net: only monitor select exceptions while connecting
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
>
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by only adding a socket to the `select()` exception set while waiting for a non-blocking `connect()` to complete. Windows needs that to detect a failed connection. Established connections no longer monitor the exception set on any platform. This approach was suggested by theuni in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#issuecomment-6931290348 and replaces the earlier version of this PR, which ignored the exception set outside Windows and disconnected on it on Windows.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes one additional change for clarity: if `errorSet` is reported for a socket we did not request to read from, disconnect directly instead of first attempting a send that would fail (emits a different log message). `if (recvSet || errorSet)` is left as is. Since `select()` no longer reports errors for established connections, this only applies to `poll()`.

Test coverage is introduced in `p2p_socket_errors.py`.

Finally the same early error check is applied to HTTP, with urgent data coverage in `interface_http.py`.

pulls.title: test: check guarantees of bech32 error detection
pulls.body:
This adds bech32 checks around the limits of bech32 strings, and the guarantees, as well as the limitations, of bech error detection.

The first commit adds those tests:
- validity of a bech32 string at the base max length, and invalidity after that
- validity of a bech32 string at the length limit for silent payment addresses (1023)
- failing checksums after 1-4 changes for length 90
- show that after 5 changes another valid checksum might exist
- failing checksum after 1-3 changes for length 1023
- show that after 4 changes another valid checksum might exist
- Show that LocateErrors can locate up to 2 errors
- Show that LocateErrors might locate a different solution to get a valid checksum

Second commit just modifies comments about error detection 'guarantees' around bech32 length limit constants. I think the formulation 'Guarantees finding up to N errors' is ambiguous.
Someone might interpret it as 'fixes up to N errors', but it's not. It's not even 'Locates up to N errors', since LocateErrors() can find up to 2 errors. Now with the new 1023 length, LocateError can't even anymore guarantee finding the correct 2 errors (2 errors in one direction, 2 changes tried in the other direction, and we are beyond the 3 changes that guarantee there is no other possible valid checksum).
So I think the comments should only say 'The checksum can detect up to N changes' instead, not guarantee more.

Context : 
Initially I was just looking at all code around Silent Payments, looked if the bech32 test had been updated to have tests for the new CharLimit::SILENT_PAYMENTS, and saw less tests than I expected.

With the change on #36895 : 
> libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes O(n) in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become O(n^2).

This adds `btck_witness_stack_get_items` which reads the stack in one O(n) pass and writes each item's pointer and size into two arrays passed to it. `WitnessStackApi::GetItems` is the C++ wrapper. The pointers are valid as long as the witness stack exists.

An earlier version passed each item to a callback from the bottom of the stack to the top. That order followed the serialization, which can only be read from the bottom up, more than how a stack should actually be read. This version lets the items be read from either end.

pulls.title: kernel: Add script evaluation tracer
pulls.body:
This adds a callback hook to the kernel library C header for getting the current script evaluation state on each script evaluation step. This can be used for debugging scripts and gives external applications a view into how Bitcoin Core does script evaluation.

The initial sketch for this work was prepared on rust-bitcoinkernel: https://github.com/sedited/rust-bitcoinkernel/tree/feature_script_debug . That branch also includes a very rudimentary script debugger showcasing the use case for this patch. Clankers seems to do a decent job at coding up prototypes for more featureful debuggers, which seems like a fun project to hack on if anybody else wants to give it a try.

This feature is gated behind the ENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE flag. To compile with the feature enabled, pass `-DENABLE_SCRIPT_TRACE=ON`. If the feature is not manually enabled, the trace hooks are stubbed out.

The traces are divided into separate frames. RAII is used to guarantee that every script evaluation has at least its start and end state captured. Each instruction generates a unique frame as well.

The ScriptError in the VerifyScript invocation run when calling script_pubkey_verify is added in order to be able to surface the error code in the trace frames.

Another use case could also be using the frames to ensure that the script interpreter is actually doing what we think it is doing during the script tests. This might prevent unit test bugs in the future, i.e. when [error conditions shadow actual behaviour](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33961), and could also be interesting for fuzzing the script interpreter.

pulls.title: test: split `CreateNewBlock_validity` into independent test cases
pulls.body:
`CreateNewBlock_validity` mines a 110-block chain and then runs four subtests on it as member functions. The subtests share one chain, so each starts from whatever the previous one left behind, and the caller has to patch `Tip()->nHeight` between them. Inside `TestBasicMining` a single `CMutableTransaction` is reused across all sections, with each section overwriting some of its fields, so the transaction a section actually tests depends on every section before it.

This PR removes both kinds of hidden state.

pulls.title: test: Add test for CompactSize larger than MAX_SIZE value
pulls.body:
Currently there is no test coverage for oversized CompactSize. This is fine, because a vector this large will already be rejected earlier by the P2P transport payload size check.

However, it would be good to still add test coverage:

* Removing the check would pass all tests.
* There is some accidental non-deterministic coverage through tx-deser "fuzzing", which hurts coverage reports, see https://github.com/corecheck/corecheck/pull/219#discussion_r4554170963.
* Having explicit end-to-end P2P coverage for such corrupt messages seems fine.

pulls.title: mining: add Block interface, fix template data race
pulls.body:
This PR catches two birds with one stone:

- fixes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36515
- adds a `Block` interface, which lets IPC clients fetch the block data (or its header)

This means a client can still fetch (and store) the block after `submitSolution()`, but we no longer mutate the template's `CBlock` for this.

### Block interface

`submitSolution()` no longer modifies the template. It applies the solution to a copy of the template block and returns a `Block` handle for that copy, also when the block is rejected.

`Mining::submitBlock()` and `BlockTemplate::block()` do the same. The new interface has a `data()`, `header()` and `coinbaseMerklePath()` method, so these are migrated from the `BlockTemplate` interface.

The interface can be expanded later, e.g. to tell whether the block is part of the active chain (or went stale, useful for a miner to know).

This is a breaking change for IPC clients:

- `getBlockHeader()` → `block().header()`
- `getBlock()` → `block().data()`
- `getCoinbaseMerklePath()` → `block().coinbaseMerklePath()`
- `bool submitSolution(..., reason, debug)` → `Block submitSolution(..., accepted, reason, debug)`
- `bool submitBlock(block, reason, debug)` → `Block submitBlock(block, accepted, reason, debug)`

It uses new ordinals and old methods throw.

`submitSolution()` now throws when the coinbase is null, instead of returning false.

### Performance

My agent measured how long after `submitSolution()` sv2-tp forwards the next template, with master as the baseline and an adapted sv2-tp as the client:

| Workload | Master | This PR | Paired median difference (95% CI) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Empty block | 1.32 ms | 1.40 ms | +0.05 ms [−0.11, +0.15] |
| Near-full block, 3.7 MB | 10.11 ms | 10.07 ms | −0.09 ms [−0.44, +0.28] |

The extra `block()` call costs about 0.15 ms per template for a C++ client. The alternative approach of having `submitSolution()` return the full `CBlock` added 6ms.

pulls.title: kernel: let callers create the block manager
pulls.body:
The kernel creates its block storage inside `btck_chainstate_manager_create`, configures it through the chainstate manager's options and reads blocks through the chainstate manager. Pruning (#35627) needs block storage that the caller can configure, keep and prune directly.

This adds `btck_BlockManagerOptions` and `btck_BlockManager`. `btck_chainstate_manager_create` takes a block manager and keeps a shared reference to it, so either handle can be destroyed first. A block manager can be passed to only one chainstate manager, and a failed creation still uses it up unless the contexts differ. `btck_block_read` and `btck_block_spent_outputs_read` take the block manager, and block tree entries are valid for its lifetime, which can be longer than the chainstate manager's.

Changes for callers:
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_create` no longer takes a blocks directory.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_wipe_dbs` is replaced by `btck_block_manager_options_update_wipe_block_tree_db` and `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_wipe_chainstate_db`. The block tree db is wiped when the block manager is created, and wiping it also wipes the chainstate db, which the old function required anyway.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_block_tree_db_in_memory` moves to the block manager options.
- Both options objects take the same total database cache, and each uses its own share.

Based on #36739. Draft until it is merged. Feedback on the API is welcome in the meantime.

pulls.title: qa: assert_equals -> assert_true/assert_false
pulls.body:
Instead of this in the functional tests:
```python
    assert_equals([long expression pushing next arg to the right], True)
    assert_equals([other long expression pushing next arg to the right], False)
```
we get:
```python
    assert_true([long expression without arg on the right side..])
    assert_false([other long expression without next arg to the right.])
```

The main point of this change is that `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` reduce cognitive tokens when scanning the code (equals to *what*...?). (As a consequence, `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` are also common in other test frameworks).

`assert_equals()` continues to be used in cases where we don't compare to boolean literals.

`assert_true([expression])` is different from plain `assert [expression]` in that `assert` is truthy while `assert_true` requires boolean `True`. (`assert` can also be deactivated when executing Python code in optimized mode (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30529#discussion_r1893029530)).

A smaller scale attempt at introducing `assert_true()` was originally included in #31874 before being dropped.

pulls.title: kernel: add manual pruning
pulls.body:
Part of #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111. The kernel can't open a data directory that a pruned node created, and it has no way to prune.

This adds a prune option on the block manager, `btck_block_manager_prune_up_to_height` and `btck_chainstate_manager_flush`. With the option set, the kernel opens pruned data directories. The chainstate manager created with the block manager decides what may be deleted, so pruning fails without one.

Pruning writes only block storage, never the chainstate. After an unclean shutdown the chainstate on disk is at the last flush, and recovering from there needs the blocks above it. Pruning therefore keeps every block above the fork point between the last flushed block and the active chain, and reports `btck_PruneStatus_NEEDS_FLUSH` when that bound limited what it could delete. The caller can flush and prune again.

The fork point matters when the flushed block was reorged out. Recovery then disconnects the stale blocks, which needs their block and undo data, and connects the new ones from their block data. `btck_block_manager_prune_reorg_tests` covers that case and fails if the bound uses the flushed block's height instead.

A fast prune option lets tests prune, since test chains never fill a 128 MiB block file.

Based on #36738 and #36854. Draft until both are merged.

pulls.title: refactor: break the blockstorage/validation circular dependency
pulls.body:
`node/blockstorage.cpp` includes `validation.h`, and the lint lists `node/blockstorage -> validation -> node/blockstorage` as an expected circular dependency. This removes it, and the lint confirms the cycle is gone.

The largest user of validation in block storage is `ImportBlocks`, which drives validation. It moves to `node/chainstate` and sets the reindex flag through the new `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()`, which writes the flag to the block tree database and sets the in-memory flag under one `cs_main` hold. The last commit moves `FatalError` to `kernel/fatal_error.h`, after which `blockstorage.cpp` no longer includes `validation.h`. `validation.h` still exports `FatalError` for its other users.

Validation also reaches into `BlockManager`'s private members as a friend. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping `m_check_for_pruning` and `m_dirty_blockindex` non-public. Both require `cs_main`, and the annotations let the compiler check it. After this, nothing outside `BlockManager` writes its private state or the block tree database.

There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36738. Draft until it is merged.

Thanks to musaHaruna, who [suggested `RequestPrune()`](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#discussion_r4283138022) in his review on my fork. The flag marks a pending pruning check, so callers request it and storage decides whether anything qualifies, which keeps the flag private once the friend declarations are gone.

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric configuration options now reject values that are out of range instead of silently wrapping or inverting. Previously a negative value could disable the intended limit entirely.

  - `-dbbatchsize` and `-dbcrashratio` must be non-negative. A negative `-dbbatchsize` wrapped to a huge value and disabled batch flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch in memory.
  - `-limitclustersize`, `-limitancestorcount`, `-limitdescendantcount`, `-mempoolexpiry`, `-datacarriersize`, `-maxsendbuffer`, `-maxreceivebuffer`, `-bantime`, `-bytespersigop` and `-maxtipage` must be non-negative.
  - `-limitclustercount` must be between 1 and 64.
  - `-timeout` must be positive. It previously fell back to the default silently, unlike the analogous `-peertimeout`, which already errored.

  Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": `-dbbatchsize=0`,
  `-limitclustersize=0`, `-datacarriersize=0`, `-mempoolexpiry=0`,
  `-maxtipage=0`, `-bytespersigop=0`, `-maxsendbuffer=0`,
  `-maxreceivebuffer=0` and `-bantime=0`.

- The `-help` output for `-bytespersigop`, `-datacarriersize`, `-dbbatchsize`, `-stopatheight` and `-checkblockindex` now shows the `=<n>` placeholder for their value, matching how they are actually parsed.

pulls.title: Detect transaction problems early during deserialization
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521 (and not included in #36895), as it's effectively an independent improvement.

This introduces a number of additional checks that are applied during transaction deserialization, which reduce various worst case deserialization time scenarios:
* Reject transactions with more txins or more txouts than can possibly fit in a block (applied always)
* Reject transactions with 0 txins or 0 txouts (applied in P2P code only; there are RPCs like `fundrawtransaction` that explicitly support transactions with 0 inputs)
* Count weight accurately during transaction or block deserialization, and bail out as soon as it exceeds 4M (applied in P2P code).

This is a mild behavior change, as detecting these problems early causes them to be treated as deserialization errors, which in P2P logic cause messages to be ignored instead of peer disconnection.

pulls.title: wallet: Only broadcast resubmitted transactions that were added to the mempool
pulls.body:
As discussed in #36403, one of the issues with current rebroadcast behavior is that the rebroadcast begins an unconditional relay of a transaction to peers. While this is broadcast is limited to peers that have not previously been inv'd the transaction, there is still a privacy leak in this double relay of a transaction, especially so for transactions that are still in nodes' mempools.

This PR changes the rebroadcast to only rebroadcast transactions if the transaction was not already present in our mempool. This provides some additional privacy while retaining intended rebroadcast behavior as transactions that have likely fallen out of nodes' mempools are the ones that actually need to be rebroadcast.

The wallet rebroadcast tests are additionally refactored for isolation so that their behaviors can still be tested after this change. Additionally, a test for the loading resubmission was added, as well as a test for the new behavior.

pulls.title: validation: Ensure Invalid ValidationState has result
pulls.body:
Block and transaction validation results are represented in `ValidationState`, and invalid results in "Invalid" states. Invalid validation results have a `result`, an enum value, and a `reject_reason`, a structured string.

The change is to ensure that an __invalid result always has a set result and reject reason__. This increases code robustness/security.

One instance was identified where the result was not set, and is being fixed by a new `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result. PR #31981 moved a previous-block check from outside of `TestBlockValidity()` to inside it, and introduced a new usage of `BlockValidationState` with unset result. The result field is not checked outside. This instance is changed now to use the newly-introduced `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` value.

The new enum value is added to the kernel C API and its C++ wrapper. In P2P, a `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result does not lead to punishing the peer.

A few test-only instances with empty reject reason are changed to use a dummy value ("dummy-reason").

History: this was found on the side of #35570, but left untouched there; see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-5739477357 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#discussion_r4075379069.

pulls.title: init: Fix surprising behaviors of negated options
pulls.body:
While looking into #36759 I discovered `-notorcontrol` did the opposite of what would be expected from it and I then checked for similar issues in other init options. There are several more where `-nofoo` does something surprising including one of them crashing the node.

This PR attempts to fix all these surprising behaviors while also keeping things as simple as possible and just change behavior to something that makes sense harmless in the context of the option. Fixes that use a common approach for the fix are grouped together into a commit even if the options included themselves may have no relation at all.

| Commit | Problematic options behavior | Fix approach |
|---|---|---|
| [mempool: Reject cluster limits below 1](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/512773d111daaa4330c873ed5889b9ef511f6e3a) | `-nolimitclustercount` hits an assertion in `TxGraph` on the first mempool transaction. `-nolimitclustersize` rejects every transaction. | Reject values below 1 at startup. |
| [args: Add NEGATE_TO_EMPTY so -nofoo reads as an empty string](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/ac4b8feb3fe151d1b00085cfe15a856ccede6e6e) | `GetArg()` returns `"0"` for a negated option. The `-no*notify` options run the command `0`, `-nosigner` uses `0` as signer, `-noi2psam` fails startup and `-norpcpassword` sets the password to `0`. Opt-in because options like `-noonion` and `-noblockfilterindex` depend on reading `"0"`. | New opt-in flag `NEGATE_TO_EMPTY` makes `GetArg()` return `""`. |
| [init: Read -cjdnsreachable and -help as booleans](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/dc4ddbacf791ac6742261bf66dcf42887bfb74ff) | `-cjdnsreachable=0` and `-nocjdnsreachable` turn CJDNS on. `-nohelp` prints the help. | Use `GetBoolArg()` instead of `IsArgSet()`. |
| [args, wallet: Fix empty and negated -blocksdir and -walletdir](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/be71581c2fc65722f6e335e6506cda342eb23ef7) | `-noblocksdir` writes block files relative to the working directory. `-nowalletdir` fails startup. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. An empty value falls back to the default directory, like `-datadir` does. |
| [init: Require -nolistenonion with -notorcontrol](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/44b1c5b05057bf3a768eac63922c085163975dcc) | `-notorcontrol` connects to `0.0.0.0:9051`, which reaches a local Tor. | Fail at startup unless `-listenonion` is disabled. |
| [init: Disallow negating options where it has no meaning](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/6447b07919072f12aba36313814fd4962dd4363a) | `-nocheckblocks`, `-nomaxreceivebuffer`, `-nomaxsendbuffer` and `-nomaxtipage` read as 0, the opposite of what the user asked for. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. |

`-nomempoolexpiry` has a similar kind of problem. It evicts transactions as soon as the next one arrives. I left it out because #36540 already is open and addresses this.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: test: [NOMERGE,SKETCH] Add thread-safe fast-failing test macros
pulls.body:
Currently, the unit tests use different boost check macros. However, this is problematic:

* The check macros are tied to the boost test framework and can not be used in other tests, such as the fuzz tests.
* The check macros are not overflow-safe. For example `BOOST_CHECK_GT(-10, 10U);` compiles and passes fine, even though it is obviously wrong.
* The check macros are not thread-safe. Using them in a thread will compile fine, but then fail tsan later on. Usually it is trivial to replace them by a plain `assert`, but it would be better if the macros just worked under tsan.
* The check macros are not fast-failing. This is confusing, as the test continues to run and will print more logs, making it harder to spot the first failure. Also, it is contrary to the internal check macros `assert` and `Assert`, and even `CHECK_NONFATAL` under debug mode, which all lead to an immediate abort.

Fix all issues by adding new check macros: `ASSERT`, `ASSERT_EQ` (and friends), `ASSERT_EQ_COLLECTIONS` (C++20 range-based), as well as `ASSERT_EXCEPTION`. They can be used as a drop-in replacement for the corresponding boost macro.

The implementation for all macros is only ~150 LOC, so it should be preferable to any external dependency addressing the above issues (which I couldn't find anyway).

(Tracking issue: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34666)

### Note on naming (why `ASSERT`?)

The test macros follow the naming and semantics of the internal Bitcoin Core macros (`assert`, and `Assert`). While it may confusing to have three unary `assert` macros that do *roughly* the same, it should be harmless and any macro that compiles is fine to use. (There is a special edge case to `Assert`, which allows to be turned into an exception as part of `g_detail_test_only_CheckFailuresAreExceptionsNotAborts`, but this shouldn't matter much).

In theory, if devs didn't care about nice diagnostic messages on a failure (printing the left and right side), the macros could even be a direct alias of `assert` or `Assert`, reducing the LOC even more. Though, I think it is fine and preferable to have slightly better failure messages in tests.

Also, the naming and semantics follow the Bitcoin Core functional test macros, which also start with `assert_`.

### Later optimizations

The macros are currently sitting in the header, but once they are applied to the whole codebase, the pretty-printing implementation can move to a cpp file, which reduces the weight of the header and makes it possible to change or add pretty-printing features without a whole re-compilation of all tests.

pulls.title: rpc: refactor: use string_view in Arg/MaybeArg
pulls.body:
The `RPCHelpMan::{Arg,MaybeArg}` helpers avoid copying (potentially) large strings by returning them as `const std::string*` (`MaybeArg`) or `const std::string&` (`Arg`). For `MaybeArg`, this has the not-so-nice effect that users need to deal with raw pointers, potentially also requiring new functions (e.g. [`EnsureUniqueWalletName` ](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32845/commits/d127b25199118756122232d9aafff19f1922869b#diff-d8bfcfbdd5fa7d5c52d38c1fe5eeac9ce5c5a794cdfaf683585140fa70a32374R32)) with raw pointers being implemented.

This PR aims to improve on this by returning a trivially copyable `std::string_view` (`Arg`) or `std::optional<std::string_view>` (`MaybeArg`), modernizing the interface without introducing any additional copying overhead. In doing so, it also generalizes whether we return by value or by pointer/reference using `std::is_trivially_copyable_v` instead of defining the types manually.

In cases where functions currently take a `const std::string&` and it would be too much work / touching consensus logic to update them (`signmessage.cpp`), a `std::string` copy is made (which was already happening anyway).

The last 2 commits increase usage of the `{Arg,MaybeArg}<std::string_view>` helpers, and could be dropped/pruned if anything turns out to be controversial - I just think it's a nice little cleanup.

This adds a `requestedOutputs` field to `BlockCreateOptions` which lets the Mining IPC client request outputs to be added before the consensus mandatory commitments.

The main use case is being able to add `OP_RETURN` outputs for merged mining without patching `BlockAssembler::CreateNewBlock()`.

It could potentially also be used to make payouts directly from the coinbase, but this is unsafe for any amount above the subsidy (this PR adds checks for that). In general a pool should add payout outputs _after_ obtaining the block template, even a solo pool.

Although it's possible to modify pool software to add merge mining outputs on top of the returned block template (e.g. by intercepting and modifying the Stratum v2 `NewTemplate` message), it may in practice be easier to do this when requesting a template.

pulls.title: ci: Consistenly only cache on the default branch
pulls.body:
Fixes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/33685

The general idea for caches is to only save them on pushes to the default branch, because the cache is limited in size and time that the only benefit of the cache can be to speed up pull requests against the default branch.

Backport pull requests to older branches don't benefit from caches, because usually they will be running into a cache miss anyway. Also, they would cause the cache size to overflow and lead to cache misses down the line.

So fix it by consistently applying cache saves only on the default branch.

For reference, the same is already done for the composite action in this repo: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/2444488f6ad32dcbbed51a73cd4f59ff3a239e32/.github/actions/save-caches/action.yml#L15

pulls.title: clang-format: Set PackConstructorInitializers: CurrentLine
pulls.body:
Now that the minimum supported clang version is larger than 14, the `PackConstructorInitializers` setting can be set to `CurrentLine` in the clang-format file. (This option was added in clang 14. Ref: https://releases.llvm.org/17.0.1/tools/clang/docs/ClangFormatStyleOptions.html#packconstructorinitializers)

The `CurrentLine` option will either put all constructor initializers on the current line if they fit. Otherwise, it will put each one on its own line.

The `CurrentLine` option is desirable over the current `BinPack` option, because:

* It is what the majority of the codebase is currently using.
* It makes it easier to skim the lines to ensure all fields are properly initialized, without having to parse bin-packed constructor initializers, possibly with nested initializer lists, function calls, or ternary operators.
* It makes diffs smaller when an initializer is added or removed, because only a single line is touched. Otherwise, the whole bin-packed block could re-flow, making the diff harder to parse.

Note: The previous `BinPack` option allows any formatting, due to the current `ColumnLimit: 0`. I presume developers manually formatted most constructor initializers to be on separate lines? With the new `CurrentLine` setting, one has to only put the first initializer on a separate line, and clang-format will take care of the rest.

For example:

```sh
echo 'A::A(O o)
: m_first{o.a, o.b},
  m_second{fun(o)}, m_third{o.c?o.d:o.e} {}' | clang-format --style=file:./src/.clang-format
```

Will put each on a separate line. Previously, it was left as-is.

pulls.title: test: avoid BSD ephemeral-port collisions in HTTP clients
pulls.body:
While stress-testing #36147 I noticed sporadic port collisions still occurring on FreeBSD.

`set_ephemeral_port_range()` keeps the source port out of the test port range, but only for sockets the framework creates itself. Python's `http.client` creates its sockets internally, so RPC and REST connections can still be given a source port inside the test range. A connection to a closed port can then connect to itself. For example, the wrong-RPC-port startup check failed with `BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1` because the client read back its own request.

This change adds a `netutil.HTTPConnection` subclass that sets the port range before connecting, and uses it in `AuthServiceProxy` and in the tests that open HTTP connections directly.

HTTPS is left unchanged because we don't serve RPC over TLS so it seems unnecessary.

pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.
